utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, having consulted the accused and discussed the matter, I have given up asking any questions because they are not of any special importance. So I won't be asking any questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kupreskic. My name is Franck Terrier. I'm one of the Prosecution attorneys, and, as I'm sure you've been told, I'm going to ask you a few questions further to your testimony of yesterday. First of all, I would like to know whether you kept any kind of record or log of the events you experienced during the war?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I asked you the question because yesterday you gave us a great deal of detailed information, and your memories apparently were very detailed. My first question has to do with the relationship that you had with the Muslims who lived in Ahmici. You told us, of course, that the relationship was excellent, and I would like to know, however, whether that relationship didn't change unfavourably during 1992 and 1993. If so, I would like you to explain to us why that happened.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, there was no deterioration in the relations with the people that I had been special friends with, especially with my godfathers or kum. Particularly with next door neighbours, we would go to restaurants together and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could we say that the lower mosque in Ahmici, the one with the minaret, in 1990, let us say, if I'm not wrong, did that not give rise to discussions? Didn't that change the climate among the communities in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that for the simple reason that many Croats, to Mr. Hasim Ahmic who had built his private mosque, had helped him, first of all, to get all the necessary papers and documents necessary to build the mosque. He also had a certain amount of difficulty with regard to his own people from Upper or Gornji Ahmici. When construction was under way of the minaret itself, he was not able to find the necessary quantities of nails that he needed, a large quantity of these nails. I personally bought the nails for him in Kakanj, and I presented them to him as a donation for the mosque. Let me add to that the following fact: When the mosque was opened, a lot of invitations were sent out to the Croats as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Were you yourself there when the mosque was inaugurated?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I was personally present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, yesterday you said that the population of Ahmici had doubled in 1993, that is, the beginning of 1993, because of the influx of refugees. Is it correct to say that these refugees, who settled in Ahmici in large numbers, were mostly Muslims?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, with the fall of Jajce, from Jajce, both the Croats and Muslims left, and all of them stayed for about a day or two in the region of Vitez. However, many Croats who were expelled from their own homes, quite simply, did not wish to remain there in Vitez, so they continued their journey towards Tomislavgrad and Herzegovina. However, the Muslim people, practically all of them, remained in the area of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But, Mr. Kupreskic, how can you explain the phenomena that Croatian refugees did not settle in the region of Vitez, not in Ahmici, that they would go to Tomislavgrad or even further to Herzegovina, whereas the Muslim refugees, they did settle in Central Bosnia? How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know how to explain that fact. I myself at that time gave the two houses belonging to my brothers because Didaci had not fallen yet, the village of Didaci from which refugees came later on. They only stayed for two or three days and then went on towards Tomislavgrad and Herzegovina. Some of them went to Croatia. Others went abroad to Deutschland, Germany, to Holland, wherever they had any relations or friends, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: However, in the region of Central Bosnia, around Busovaca or Vitez, the refugees, as you demonstrated yesterday, easily were able to find a place to stay, that they could obtain help from friends or members of their families. That isn't what led them to go further away. Could we say that the explanation can be found in the political climate or the ethnic composition of Central Bosnia at that time? Is that the explanation for the desire of the Croatian refugees to go further and not to stop in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, I would like us to speak about your professional activity, specifically, the business that you were responsible for at that time in the Vitez region. First of all, it seems to me that in the city of Vitez itself you were running a restaurant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When you left the area with your wife and children, that is, when you left Vitez to go to Germany, what arrangements did you make for running the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In view of the fact that my wife's brother was also in the catering business, at that time when I left with my wife and children for Germany, I left the restaurant to him, my brother-in-law, to run the restaurant, and he ran it until the very beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But you yourself, you remained the owner; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remained the owner; however, he rented the restaurant from me, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Does that restaurant still exist today?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It exists to the present day, and today it is run by my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let's speak now about the company whose first name was Stefani-Bosna, and then after 1992, it changed to another name. We have a document that shows the change of name of the business, which was tendered yesterday as D23/3. I would like you to tell us why you changed the name of the business.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I changed the name of my business because I stopped working with Greece, and we had been in a partnership. I formed the company and gave it the name of Stefani because we worked with Greece a lot. Then I changed the name to Sutra because we were all referred to by the nickname of Sutra.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You mean that the Greek company you worked with was called Stefani; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Stefani Athens. There was Stefani Ljubljana, which was run by Mr. Dusan Sever, and I formed the Stefani-Bosna company in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understand. Could you tell us, speaking about the Sutra company, what was its legal structure and what specific role did Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic play at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Vlatko Kupreskic was in the SPS in Vitez. He was an economist by profession. In view of the fact that the company, quite simply, its business dropped off, he was sent home to wait for more work. I wanted to take advantage of his professional capabilities, as he is, as I say, a graduated economist and worked in the firm, and so I took him into my own company. After several jobs that he had done for me, I appointed him co-partner of the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But what was the legal structure of that business? Was it a corporation with limited responsibility or was it an individual company? I'd like to know exactly what legal category it falls in. I believe that this can be explained under Croatian law.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was a company with full liability.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The capital, the capital of the company, among which people was it distributed?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, the capital was exclusively my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: At some point, before 1993 or after April 1993, did Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic become one of the owners of that company?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He only became co-owner when he built a facility, what we referred to as Veleprodaja in Ahmici, the warehouse for wholesale goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What was the main activity of that company? We're speaking about the period 1992, the end of 1992, the beginning of 1993. What was the main activity of Sutra?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: For the most part, it was for the sale of mixed types of goods, that is to say, food stuffs, clothing, and generally goods of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Where did you buy the merchandise?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We bought the merchandise in Croatia, for the most part, as well as in Herzegovina, and we added on to our assortment from Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: To whom did you sell this merchandise? How did you sell it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We sold the merchandise to all buyers, both as wholesale and retail.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Is it possible to have an idea of the amount of your sales, your sales figures, the total amount of purchasing that you did over the year; is that possible?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, about, let me say, approximately 200.000 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Over a year; right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In '93 -- no, '92, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So in 1992, can we say --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In 1992, did the company make a profit?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: A large profit? Could you give us an idea of what the profit was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was a long time ago, so I couldn't tell you exactly, but there was profit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How did the financial situation of Sutra develop in 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, in 1993, we continued to work normally right up until the 15th of April, that is to say, the 16th of April, when all work stopped, all activity stopped. That is to say, all activities carried on normally until then. We made no balance sheets or anything like that because the war interrupted everything. All we did was to see that the goods that were left at the beginning of the war that we had on our hands, that we solved that somehow, and our idea was to turn the goods into money because the army, in part, took some of our goods away from us in the form of foodstuffs, mostly, and cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that in 1992 and 1993 you were a prosperous businessman in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, we could say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Is it correct that in 1994, shortly after the conflict, you once again became prosperous, that prosperity that you had developed through your commercial activities to a large extent? And I refer to what you said yesterday referring to imports from the entire world of a large number of sheep.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I began working straight afterwards, sometime in April 1994, and the development of events was such that at the time, the prices were extremely high in Central Bosnia and not everybody was able to go and buy goods elsewhere. So we returned fairly quickly to the level we had beforehand. As far as the sheep are concerned, the sheep that I imported from Australia in 1996, the Rijaset of the Islamic community opened an accreditation directly with the Bavag Bank in Vienna, and for the Australian bank, a letter of credit to the Australian bank in Sydney which would be transferred, it was transferable, which meant that we imported the sheep with the funds from the Rijaset of the Islamic community. The transportation of it, itself, the Alfares Shipping Company from Freemantle port to the port of Ploce cost 1.600.000 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We could then say, if I look at the numbers that you've just given us, that today you are a significant businessman, an important businessman?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let's go back to 1992, beginning of 1993. I would like you to explain to us what relationship you had with the HVO authorities for the conduct of your business.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that I did not have any great problems. Whenever I needed anything, any type of permit to travel, for example, and to go and get the goods, I would get this authorisation without any problems. This is borne out by the fact that I was the best supplier of the type of preserves that I produced for the whole of the municipality in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We therefore could even say that you had excellent relations with the HVO authorities?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Who were the people who were responsible -- who were the officials in the HVO that you had contacts with? What were their names?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the time, there was Mr. Ivica Santic; he was the mayor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes. However, in the economic sphere, or in supplies, there were other people who were responsible?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, Dragan -- I can't remember his surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. Did you have competition at that time in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How is it that you were able to replace your competitors so easily with the people in charge of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it was like this, you see: Some companies, even bigger companies, were engaged in other activities. I exclusively dealt with foodstuffs. There were other companies on a par with me, but not many like that. However, the market is such that the one who offers the best prices wins.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In order to be so well considered by the HVO authorities, weren't there certain conditions that had to be satisfied?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, of course, conditions existed. First of all, that you can supply good quality goods, that you respect all the terms, and, of course, that the payment should be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you often go outside, travel outside of Bosnia? I'm talking about the second quarter of 1992.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did, often.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Where would you go for your business?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I would go on business trips, most often to Croatia and to Herzegovina, in view of the fact that I obtained most of my goods in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When you came back to Ahmici on the 19th of October, 1992, you told us yesterday that you had come back from Split at that point and that you had discovered that there was a checkpoint at Ahmici. Were you coming back from that kind of a business trip?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all -- oh, you're referring to the 19th of October? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, the 19th of October.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I was on my way back from Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Were you alone during that trip?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I was alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Ordinarily, when you would travel to Split on business or to go to Croatia, would you go alone?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It all depended. Sometimes I went alone and sometimes Vlatko went with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Why would Vlatko Kupreskic accompany you? Was there a specific reason?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yes. In view of the fact that he was a graduated economist, he had a number of friends with whom he had connections in those companies, and, of course, because of his friendships. This helped us to do business.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could one have an idea about how frequently you would travel to Croatia at that time? Once a month, or twice a month, or what?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, on the average, it was at least once a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Had you ever been convicted for something?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You don't remember having been convicted in 1985?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I apologise. It was a suspended sentence. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Why were you convicted? For what?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I was sentenced because at that time there was a fuel shortage, and I was running a restaurant between Zenica and Zepce, and there was a terrible shortage. My house was about 50 kilometres away from the restaurant. A friend of mine offered some fuel from a tank; it was about 120 litres of gas. Because I had to, I bought this petrol. After that, the police arrived because someone had reported me, and I was taken to court in Zavidovici, and I was given a suspended sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So it was for theft, that sentence was for theft; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kupreskic, let's speak about the circumstances under which your family and yourself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Terrier. Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecutor obviously has precise data as to why the witness was sentenced because the document that he has mentions the number of the article under which he was sentenced. So I would like the Prosecutor to state the legal article because it would not be theft; it would be concealment. The difference is that he bought goods which he had reason to know were stolen because the goods were stolen by the driver of the tank truck and not by him. This is a milder crime under the legislation which was then in force in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: If I may only say briefly, with regards to the suspended sentence. The suspended sentences awarded in 1985 have been rendered null and void, and in our country, the persons who were sentenced in that year are allowed to say that they have never been sentenced, under the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps you could give us the essential elements of that criminal record, that is, having to do with the sentence because, in principle, any questions having to do with the criminal record of a witness are not relevant unless the party questioning the witness explains why. What is the relevance of the question being asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, by asking the question of the witness, I believe that the witness has given us enough information. What I was looking for was to help the Trial Chamber -- perhaps I did it in a clumsy manner. If I did, please excuse me -- it was in order to evaluate the credibility of the witness. The witness told us that, in fact, he had been convicted for theft in 1985 and that the sentence had been suspended. I am not placing any greater importance on it than that. I would like to tell Mr. Radovic that the legal article on the basis of which the witness was convicted is Article 147, paragraph 1, unless I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I can say at once that the offence was concealment and not theft. He bought goods which he had reason to know were stolen, so he was not the direct perpetrator of the theft. He only bought the goods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, do you have any documents about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need to do it now, but perhaps in due course you could produce them and give them to the Defence too, and then the matter would be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, I'd like to speak now about the departure of your family and yourself into Germany in March of 1992. You told us that the decision had been taken in order to ensure the safety of your family, your wife, and your children, that is, your three sons. You told us that in March of 1992 the situation in Central Bosnia was particularly uncertain, that it was threatening, and that you had the possibility of obtaining for your family a place to live in Germany. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would like for you to explain to us why the decision was taken -- that is, a year later, in April of 1993 -- to bring your entire family back to Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mostly I was moved by the fact that my youngest son told me that he was so fed up with Germany that if I didn't come and fetch him, he would jump from the third floor of the building. As I have already said, is there anything more valuable than one's child?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, I am not contesting your reasons, of course. But simply speaking, my question is the following: Your wife told us here when she testified some time back that if she came back, it is because you had ensured her that the situation had arranged itself, had settled down, and that in April of 1993, the situation was better in Central Bosnia than it had been in March 1992. What do you think about that statement of your wife's?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you this way: At that moment, the situation really had settled down. In fact, there were no problems in the area except for that first clash in Ahmici, which, in my opinion, was already behind us because many people had reconciled themselves with each other, started leading a normal life, many people were sitting in cafes, and I simply thought that there should be no more problems in future.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When you left in March of 1992, what were your intentions? Your family was supposed to settle in Essen with your brother, but as regards yourself, what was your intention? Did you plan to stay in Germany or did you plan to come back?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I planned to stay in Germany when I left with my children and my wife in March 1992. However, since my father told me about the threats that my house might be destroyed, that my property might be confiscated, I came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But you told us yesterday that you were considered as a deserter when you went to Germany. Who considered you a deserter?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the people who were members of the Croatian people considered me a deserter. Of course, I'm referring to people holding official positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Doesn't that mean that all the Croatian citizens in Central Bosnia at that time were considered as having, in fact, been mobilised? We're talking about March 1992. Therefore, at the very beginning, even before the establishment of the HVO, all Croatian citizens were considered as mobilised into the service of the Croatian nation?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it like that, and I wouldn't say that they were considered to be mobilised. However, these were simply threats made by individuals which my father heard about, and then he rang me up by telephone and told me to come back. He said, "If you don't come back, your property might be confiscated. There's a possibility you will be considered a deserter."

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you have the name of these people who threatened you or who threatened your property?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you see, my father told me this on the phone; however, he himself heard this from others. These were actually village rumours. As to specific names, I don't know because I wasn't there, and he couldn't tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: That means that the people who were threatening you, threatening your property, belonged to that village?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, they weren't from the village. They were simply from the Croatian authorities of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When you came back from Germany in May 1992, unless I'm mistaken, you told us yesterday that you contributed to humanitarian aid in Central Bosnia, specifically medicines. I would like to know by whom this operation was funded, how you obtained the required authorisations, and possibly who mandated you to carry out that mission?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: All the humanitarian aid in medicaments and vehicles was organised by my relative, Vlado Sucic, who owns a restaurant in Feldberg, but he appointed me his assistant because he needed people to drive the vehicles to Central Bosnia. We agreed that part of the medicaments should be given to Novi Travnik, and two vehicles, I was driving the Granada, should also be donated to Novi Travnik, and the rest was given to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But how was the operation financed?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A collection was made by Mr. Vlado Sucic, and the people living in Feldberg and the surrounding towns, who were from Central Bosnia, would bring their contributions, whether in medicaments or in money, in cash, at least that's what he told me. They had three people who were in charge. If someone brought cash, the money was used to buy vehicles and medicaments. If someone gave medicaments, this was sent on to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, now let's speak about the period following the first conflict, the conflict of October 1992. You spoke to us about a meeting which followed that conflict, that is, a meeting during which the return of the Muslims was decided. You told us yesterday that, during that meeting, Nenad Santic, Pero Skopljak, and Zoran Kupreskic participated. Does that mean that these three individuals, each at his own level and within his geographic sphere, was a director, a leader?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would not put it that way for the simple reason that Fuad and Junuz Berbic, who insisted upon that meeting, they were very good friends with Zoran. He is a mechanical engineer, and he worked in the same company as they did. They told Zoran, if he could, to convene a meeting with the leading figures of the municipality itself and to have some of the representatives there, and they would come anywhere that they decided to have the meeting, wherever the venue. The meeting was held on the terrace of my own house, in fact, and I learned about it when my aunt phoned me up in Vitez, in the restaurant where I was at that time, so that I joined the meeting later. Whereas Pero Skopljak was a man representing the Croatian people of the Vitez municipality, he was that kind of a representative; on the other hand, there was Sulejman Kalco, as I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You're telling us that Pero Skopljak represented the Vitez Croats. Who represented the Ahmici, Santici, and Pirici Croats?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you see, I said yesterday as well that Nenad Santic was the man who formed the HDZ in that region, and probably, I don't know exactly, but quite possibly, he was the main representative of the Croatian people in that region. I'm not quite sure. Zoran was in the role of somebody who was there to organise the meeting at the initiative of Mr. Fuad Berbic and Junuz.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what decisions were taken during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I do know that, as far as I recall, decisions were taken for the most part, that each side should work with its own people in the regions they lived in and, of course, to bring the situation back to what it was beforehand, that each man should talk to his own people so that life could go on normally, and to bring back a sort of joint guard which will stand guard at the entrance to our village. I decided to be the first representative, just to show that there were no problems as far as we were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember a decision which ordered the Muslims to give up their weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was not at the meeting in my house. I did hear that there was talk at a previous meeting of that sort of thing, I think on the first or second day after the conflict, that weapons, some four rifles were to be returned which had been seized from the army which was stopped at the barricade at the cemetery, and that a vehicle had been confiscated as well; however, the vehicle was returned and the rifles in question were not. I just heard talk of this, that is to say, it was not a subject of discussion in my own home on my own terrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But were you informed of a decision which requested or ordered the Muslims of Ahmici and Santici to give up their weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard about that decision, but I wasn't at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What do you know about that meeting during which the decision was taken, that is, the decision to order the Muslims to give up their arms?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Everything I know about it, I told you a moment ago, in fact, what I had heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore, what you know is that the decision was taken during another meeting, but you don't know who was present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that a decision of that kind was taken, but I really don't know who was present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let's speak about the guards, first, the joint guards and then the individual guards, that were carried out for the safety of those who lived in Ahmici, Santici, and Pirici. Who organised those patrols on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I don't know because when I returned from Germany, the guards already existed, and it was just up to me to become included because they had already treated me as a deserter of sorts. When they told me that I was to join the guard, I found time and went to do this duty, but it was only during the night. During the day, there were no village guards, except for the fact that there were people on duty standing by the radio transmitter, which was located in the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you yourself and your friends, your Croatian friends, when you were on patrol, were you dressed in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that only Mirko Sakic had a rifle at that time and Zdravko Vrebac on the occasion of the first conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When did you put on a uniform?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I put on a uniform sometime -- about 10 to 15 days after the first conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let's go back to 1992, the end of that year and the beginning of '93, that is, those patrols. Your cousins, Vlatko, Mirjan, and Zoran Kupreskic, were they also in the village guard?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Zoran and Mirjan were but Vlatko was not, as he was not capable of doing his military service in Yugoslavia either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Now, let's speak about April 1993 and the trip to Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would ask the usher to give the witness Defence Exhibit D24/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, the document which was given to you yesterday, this is it, are you the signatory?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. The signatory is Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Would you explain to us, perhaps you already did so yesterday, and if you did, I beg your indulgence, but I didn't really understand the explanation for this document, why this document exists. Why was this document drafted and to whom was it given?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This document -- that is to say, every person who travels on behalf of his company must have a document of this kind to justify his business travels and the costs incurred during the trip taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Is this a rule that was put into effect because of the circumstances, that is, a rule that the HVO had set up, that is, the Croatian Community, or was it a rule which already existed in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was a regulation that existed in the former Yugoslavia. On the basis of this document, a report is drawn up as to what was accomplished during the business trip taken, what business was agreed upon, and it serves for justifying the costs of the business trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did the HVO expressly maintain the regulations of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you that, whether it adhered to all the regulations, but it did to some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In the document that you have in front of you, was an authority indicated? What authority?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, the document does not specify any particular authority. This is a document of the company, a company document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, I understood that it was a company document, but it's a document which is not intended to be given to an authority, to justify authorisations; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is true, but it is submitted throughout the year. When we make a final balance at the end of the year, it goes to the incomes revenue inspection of the municipality where the company is registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Document D24/3 that you have in front of you is a copy of an original?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But wasn't the original sent to an administration, as you just said?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, the original is not sent to any administrative office. We have to have it in our own archives, in our records, so that if a control is sent, an inspector is sent from the revenue, it just sees whether everything is in order, and the document itself stays in the company by --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understand. Let's now speak about the trip from Vitez to Split. Could you remind us of the date that you left and what time, rather, you left and what time you arrived in Split? Of course, I'm not asking you to tell us the story of this trip, which you already did yesterday, but simply the date and the time.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We left on the 14th in the morning at about 6.00, and we were in Split sometime between 1.00 and 2.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What did you do when you got to Split?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We went to the marketplace where we had some friends of ours who brought in goods directly from Turkey, and, in fact, it was a question of jeans. When we went on this trip, because of my wife, we made use of it and took some of the jeans, as much as we could fit into the boot of our car. That's what we did, and then we went to collect my wife at the airport in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, what was the business transaction that you carried out at that point and would justify Vlatko Kupreskic's having gone with you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We were together in a large house, which is called Koteks in Split; it was a firm. We were discussing the purchases of large quantities of salt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: On that day in Split, you didn't only buy jeans. You also negotiated a contract for significant amounts of salt?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the Koteks Split company, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you sign any business documents?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the occasion, we discussed all the terms, but the shipment of that salt came later, 30 days later, because they were not able to cater to our requirements immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Is there a single commercial document which was drafted by one of your partners, your Croatian partners, which refers to the meeting on the 14th of April, 1993 in Split in which Vlatko Kupreskic was a participant?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. I really couldn't say whether the document exists now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In respect of these textiles, these jeans that you bought in the market, were they paid for by some kind of a bank cheque or some kind of a money order?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The jeans were paid for in cash.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Now, this business trip of the 14th of April, 1993 to Split, of that meeting, there is no bank record which has survived; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Everything we had was listed in a log that we kept related to the agreements we reached. Afterwards, we did this business with Koteks from Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I was asking you to be as specific as possible in respect of the name, the address of the company where you went to negotiate a salt contract and the names of the people that you met.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, I know that it was Koteks of Split, but I really couldn't tell you now the names of the people we met on the occasion. I would have to look it up in my notebook because it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher to give the witness Exhibit D25/3, which was tendered yesterday into the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, this document was drawn up by the HVO and signed by Marijan Skopljak. Is it right to say that Marijan Skopljak was an individual whom you knew very well?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: One could say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Is it true that the document was drawn up by the HVO at your request?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Was the request made in writing, or merely orally?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What type of written document did you provide in order to get that authorisation?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We wrote it on a memorandum, a company memorandum, requesting permission to go on a business trip for -- to conduct such-and-such business. Of course, then they would issue this permit on the basis of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When you made the request, did you specify what the dates of your business trip were to be?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in my request, state the date, and my request referred to the 13th. It was the 13th of April, for the 14th of April. Usually you would ask for a longer period of time, so if you return earlier, there would be no problems there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Are you the one who said that the date was from the 14th of April to the 24th of April?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Usually we would get about ten days for trips of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you sometimes take ten-day trips?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went for even more. I went to my family in Germany, and then I would ask for 30 days, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So the dates that are on this authorisation for travel do not imply that you had either interrupted or shortened your trip in order to come back home sooner?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sometimes we would use this same permit twice, if we, for example, went for the first time on the 14th and returned on the 17th. So that means we could go again on the 20th and come back by the 24th. But if we have not returned by the 24th, then automatically we would have problems at the various roadblocks that we encountered by the HVO. Without this document, quite simply, we were not able to travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: On the document which you have in front of you, we can see a stamp which mentions the fact that you were crossing the border at Metkovic on the 14th of April, 1993. Who put that stamp on the document?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was placed by the policemen who were at the border crossing. Sometimes they wouldn't even look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What police? Were they HVO police, or police from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: These were policemen from the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The stamp that we can see on D25/3, what direction were you going when this was put on? Had you crossed the border on the 14th of April from Bosnia into Croatia, or from Croatia into Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From Bosnia into Croatia, via Metkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When you crossed the same border, coming back at the same place, but this time from Croatia to Bosnia, were you not asked anything? Nothing at all?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we did not cross the border at the same border crossing. We crossed it at another place, called Crveni Grm, that is to say, on the road from Makarska-Vrgorac-Ljubuski. They did not stamp the document there because we were exiting from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You didn't cross the border at Metkovic, then, when you came back? That's what I've understood.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would like to ask instructions from the Trial Chamber. The Office of the Prosecutor has heard Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic, on the 11th of June, 1998, as part of Rule 64, that is, at the specific request of Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic, and in the presence of his attorneys, Mr. Krajina and Mr. Par and Mr. Gradac. The meeting was recorded on video and gave rise to a transcription of everything that had been stated by Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic on that occasion. On the same day -- that is, the 11th of June, 1998 -- a copy of the videotape was given to Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic's attorneys as is provided for in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I would like to refer to some of the statements of Vlatko Kupreskic that were given on the 11th of June, 1998, and give to your Trial Chamber the videotapes of that testimony as well as the transcript of the same hearing. I'm saying to you that shortly before the beginning of this hearing, we gave to those counsel which did not have it, the transcript of the hearing, but of course Mr. Par and Mr. Krajina, who are here, have had that since June 1998. I'm also indicating to the Trial Chamber that the questioning had to do with Vlatko Kupreskic and does not have to do with the situation of the other accused who are in this courtroom. Therefore I await the decision of Your Honours, hoping to be able to refer to certain very specific points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You referred to 64 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I meant 63.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: (In English) Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we as Vlatko Kupreskic's Defence counsel confirm everything that has been said by our esteemed colleague, the Prosecutor, as to the method of the interview and the documents and tapes which we received on that occasion. We also do not contest that these are materials which the Prosecutor has the right to use as evidence. However, we consider that at this stage of the proceedings, there is no point in presenting something that Vlatko Kupreskic said to the witness. We propose that this should be presented when Vlatko Kupreskic gives evidence and that it can be used to cast doubt on the credibility of some other witness statements, but we see no point in presenting something that Vlatko Kupreskic said to this witness today, especially since the Prosecutor has the possibility of putting questions to the witness to prove this. So we propose that the Court not permit the Prosecutor to present this material now, but that the Prosecutor might present it when the accused gives evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, very briefly, I would like to answer Mr. Par. It seems to me that in the statements that were given freely on the 11th of June, 1998, by Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic, one can find a certain number of contradictions -- flagrant ones -- in respect of what was declared by the witness before this Tribunal. This has to do with the trip to Split and the circumstances of that trip. I would like to reconcile these contradictions. Perhaps this is not the time to give the Trial Chamber that document, but I would like to be authorised to invoke these documents under the supervision of Mr. Par and Mr. Krajina, and to remind us what Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic said in order to get the point of view of the witness. If we let this occasion go by, when Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic testifies -- if he does -- we will no longer have the witness here in order to learn his point of view in respect of the statements that Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We consider that the document, at this point, should not be tendered into the record, but -- and here you are right -- it can be useful to bring out what you consider to be contradictions. But in that case, or rather in that limited framework, for you to ask questions, but to ask neutral questions, that is, without referring to the statements of Vlatko Kupreskic. That is, explicit references. Do you understand what I mean? That is, you have the document in front of you, and Defence attorneys also have the document. You can allude to it, that is, you can base yourself on the documents in order to ask questions of the witness. We consider that it would be more appropriate not to say, "Here, this is what Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic said," at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will comply with the instructions of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, could we not think that the trip from Vitez to Split and then from Split to Vitez did not last two days, but three days, and that, in fact, you spent a night in Split and a second night at that friend's house -- the friend that you spoke about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, because it wasn't like that. We arrived in Split on the first day, concluded our business, went to the airport, picked up my wife. We had an hour's drive from Split to Baska Voda, under an hour. We spent the night there because this was a good friend of ours, and we continued on our way the next day. There was no reason for us to stay two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could one not think, Mr. Kupreskic, that as regards the commercial part of the trip, that what was involved was exclusively the purchase of textiles, and that there was no question of negotiations having to do with salt?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, of course, one might think that. However, we did have these talks by the way, but simply, in the given situation, Vlatko was keeping me company so that I wouldn't have to travel alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Would it not be logical to think that, of necessity, the commercial-type documents, such as bank documents or contracts, were signed during that business trip?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, of course you might think that. We didn't conclude any contract on that day. It was only later. In fact, during the talks, we simply agreed that a month later we would conclude the deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be logical to think, under those conditions, Mr. Kupreskic, that an agreement, if there was an agreement on that day between you and your business partners, would necessarily be a draft contract, and would be referred to even if the contract was drafted a month later?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you see, it couldn't have been a month later because there was a conflict, and we were practically unable to leave the area until April '94. But on that occasion, we simply agreed in principle that in a month's time we would obtain certain quantities of salt from the salt works on Pag, the Island of Pag, through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Very well. I'm no longer referring now to the document that we spoke about a few minutes ago, but I would like to understand, Mr. Kupreskic, why Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic went with you because, according to what you said, it seems that Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic was both a negotiator, a type of negotiator that you wanted to have with you, and also that it was simply a question of -- I think you just said that a few minutes ago -- it was a question of sparing you a journey all by yourself.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, of course. First of all, I was going on a trip, and I wanted to see if we could agree on some business, and we would get some jeans, and we would also fetch my wife. Since, at that time, it was not advisable to travel alone, because there had already been murders on the part of the road between Novi Travnik and Sebesic, people were stopped and killed, especially those who had money with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore it wasn't in order to negotiate a purchase of jeans in Split that you brought Vlatko Kupreskic with you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, no, he had some friends there who brought those jeans from Turkey, and we simply went to get the jeans. We dropped into Koteks to see the people from whom we had bought goods before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you have the original of the document that you have in front of you, that is the document D26/3?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't have this document, but I think that there is a copy, that the counsel have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Isn't it possible to have the original?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't have it with me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you have it at home, at home in Bosnia, in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't have it because there is only one original of this document, and that original is somewhere with the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: It hasn't been lost? You're saying that the original has not been lost. It was given to a counsel?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it shouldn't have been. I gave it to Vlatko Kupreskic's wife because she was collecting these documents for Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic. Whether it is still in the possession of Ljubica Kupreskic or if the counsel have it, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps this is time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, you explained to us yesterday, as your wife had done before that, that afterwards you went back to a friend's house, and there you spent the night, the night of the 14th to the 15th of April, 1993. Yesterday, to a question from Mr. Par, you showed us on a map the location where you spent the night, the location where that friend lives. Here's my question: Does any type of written trace remain from that trip that you and your wife and Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic took when you stayed at the friend's house? Did you pay for a room by a bank cheque or by some kind of a credit card? Did you announce your arrival by fax or any other written method that would constitute a trace of that stay? Does that trace exist?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, for the simple reason that this person was a good friend of ours. So we just rang him up from Split and said that we would be spending the night at his house. As a friend of ours, of course, he didn't take any payment from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would like to now speak about your return on the 15th of April, 1993 to Ahmici and Santici in the late afternoon. You said that you arrived at around 5.30 in the afternoon, and at that time, you and Vlatko Kupreskic separated, and you let him off in front of his house. Did you give him any instructions for the next day, any type of professional instructions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. I think the witness said "half past six," but this can be checked in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Par is correct. Yes, unless I made a mistake, I meant "6.30." 6.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: My question of the witness is the following; I'll repeat it: Did you give Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic, on the 15th of April in the evening, did you give him any kind of professional instructions for the following day?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Along the way from Novi Travnik to Vitez, we talked about how we would leave the jeans at his house and how, on the following day, he would take some of those jeans to Travnik, to his sister's boutique. His sister lives in Travnik and has a clothing shop. We came to his house, unloaded the jeans, and my wife and I then went on to our own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How do you explain that your wife, when she testified and who I asked what you were transporting as merchandise, was unable to tell me and simply said that she didn't know and didn't see what you were transporting, whereas you just said that she helped with the unloading?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, she didn't help with the unloading. While Vlatko and I were unloading the jeans, she was saying hello to my aunt and Vlatko's wife. It wasn't such a large amount of goods for my wife to have to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us about the evening that you spent in your house together with friends and people from your family, and you mentioned many people who came to visit you, especially your wife who had returned from Germany. In front of this Trial Chamber, another witness, Mr. Mirko Sakic, made somewhat different statements in respect of the people who were present and in respect of the statements and conversations that had taken place at that point. He specifically said that Zoran and Mirjan were present but not their wives, and that Vlatko Kupreskic was present. What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what Mirko Sakic said, but I do know that certainly Zoran, Mirjan, and their wives dropped in, but Zoran's wife and Zoran stayed for a very short time because they themselves had guests at home. People came and went all the time, relatives, friends. Those closest to us came to say hello to my wife, to have a chat, and then they would go home again. They would have a drink, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You said yesterday that on the 16th of April at 4.00 in the morning, someone came knocking on your door to tell you that the Muslims were going to attack the village and that it would be appropriate to find shelter. You told us that that person was Dragan Vidovic. Could you explain to us who Dragan Vidovic was?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Dragan Vidovic was my neighbour who lives some 150 metres away from my house. He was then a member of the civil defence. Where he got the information, I really don't know, but it was he who woke me up, and then I woke my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Was Dragan Vidovic a member of an HVO military unit?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not at that time. I know that he was a member of the civil defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When he came to your door on the 16th of April at 4.00 in the morning, was he wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember because it was dark outside. He knocked on my door and he said, "Don't turn the light on." I don't remember because I really didn't see exactly what he looked like at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether he had a weapon with him?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't see that either, since he suggested that I shouldn't turn on the light.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When you left your house, your wife, your three sons, and yourself, in order to go to the shelter which had been assigned to you, how were you dressed?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was wearing a civilian uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, at that moment, I did not have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that you took your family in the direction of the Vrebac shelter but that you let them go at Ivica Vidovic's house, and then you went back to your house. How could you be sure that your family would be taken in at the shelter, to be sure in Vrebac that there would be enough room in that shelter in order to take them in?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't say I left them in Ivica Vidovic's house, but I left them near Ivica Vidovic's house because they went on in the direction of Jozo Vrebac's house. We had been in close relations with that family for a long time. I didn't even think about whether there would be room for them or not because I was simply lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How could you be sure, since you were speaking about an attack by the Muslim forces on the village, how could you be sure that the Vrebac shelter would be a safe area and that there would be no shooting that would be able to hit it and that the dangerous area was only the Ahmici area?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not know this, but I know that whenever there was any alarm, this was the largest shelter, and usually people went there. Everybody took their families there. I remember that while my family was in Germany, even then it was the case. All other shelters were much smaller.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore, when you left your family in front of Vidovic's house, you were sure that, in the shelter, they would not only be taken in but that they would be absolutely safe?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was not certain that they would be safe anywhere, but Dragan suggested that they should go over there. Perhaps he had some better information in that regard on that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that you went back on the road in the direction of your house, more specifically, in order to go to meet the refugees who lived in your brother's house, and that on the road, you met first Zoran and his family, Mirjan and his family, and that then near Mirko Sakic's house, you met soldiers. Did I understand your statement of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When returning from Ivica Vidovic's house, I first met Mirjan and Zoran's parents, and around Pudzine Kuce, I met Zoran and Mirjan with their families and saw Mirjan driving his mother-in-law in a wheelbarrow. In front of Mirko Sakic's house, since I was walking a bit faster, I caught up with this group of soldiers who were going in the direction of this warehouse. However, when I took my family to the shelter, I had already called Marica, who was at her brother Branko's, and Manda, who was in my brother Josip's house. They, at that time, declared that they had had enough of all these alarms, and they refused to go. However, when I encountered these soldiers, I realised that the situation was serious, that something could happen, and then I hurried over there to them to direct them to go to the shelter as soon as possible. I'm not sure whether I have been clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, let's go back to those soldiers you met on the road. All of you were on the same road and were walking in the same direction?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I caught up with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: All right. You caught up with them. I'm having some difficulty understanding how it was possible that at that point you didn't meet them, meet the same soldiers at that moment when you were driving your family in the direction of Vrebac.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'll tell you why, because there were at least five other paths they could have used to get to that point from other directions, not just from the part of the road I was taking. They could have come from the main road in the direction of Mirko Sakic's house or in the direction of Pudzine Kuce. They could have arrived along a path leading through the wood, which is between Mirko Sakic's house and Pudzine Kuce. They could have come from the upper side. It doesn't mean that they had to have come along the same road where I was driving my family along.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Don't you think it's logical that one would think that those soldiers had certainly come in a vehicle and that the vehicle had stopped on the road or near the road, specifically in Pirici or in Zume? Did you ever learn where their vehicle had come from?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never found out. I don't know how they arrived there. I just caught up with them at Mr. Sakic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: About how many of them were there, about?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, perhaps some -- about 30 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How were they dressed? As far as you remember, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I caught up with them, it was still dark, but I was able to notice that some had camouflage uniforms and some had black uniforms, and they were well masked with black bands and with pale blue bands on their sleeves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you recognise one or the other of them?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it was impossible to recognise these soldiers because they were very well masked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you speak to them? Did you ask them any questions about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't talk to them at all because I turned left immediately, and they went on in the direction of the warehouse. They didn't stop there, so I couldn't stop and talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that, after the meeting with the soldiers, you went back home. At that point, you called your cousin, Vlatko Kupreskic, in order to be sure that he was also going to go to a shelter and then that you went to your brother's house, your brother Josip's house. At some point during that morning or during the day of the 16th of April, did you notice or did you meet Vlatko Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I didn't meet Vlatko Kupreskic again. I only talked to him on the telephone after I had left my family, when I'd sent Marica and Manda there, and I went to try to persuade my aunt, Manda, and Marica's mother-in-law. Then I called him up to tell him I had seen a group of soldiers and that he too should take his family to a shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But subsequently, you didn't see him, and you didn't know where he had gone during that day?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Later I heard that he had gone in the direction of the shelter with his family and that only his father stayed behind in the house. He had broken his hip, and he simply refused to go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: My question doesn't have to do with what you learned, but what you personally saw that day. You did not see Vlatko Kupreskic on that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Except when I was on my way to the shelter carrying food, at one moment I saw him. I can't remember precisely whether it was at about 1.00 p.m., or in the evening, about 6.00 p.m. I don't remember when it was exactly, but I saw him in front of the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You mean the Vrebac shelter?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the Vrebac shelter, in front of the Vrebac shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In front of the shelter you saw Vlatko Kupreskic, either at 1.00 or at 6.00?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's right. I think it was at about 6.00 p.m. I think it was in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would like you to explain to us why you considered it necessary to stay where you did for most of the day -- that is, in the boiler room of your brother Josip's house -- whereas you were alone, you were near the fighting, if there was fighting, and all of your friends and members of your family were further away, either in the depression or in the various houses in Zume. Was the place where you were staying a place which seemed particularly safe to you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, at that moment, that place seemed to me to be safer than the shelter where they were. It was quite close to the gunfire, but my house was nearby. My elderly aunt and the other lady, Luca, were in the house, and that was the main reason. I saw houses burning, and I thought my house might burst into flames and then I could try to put out the fire. That was the main reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would like to understand, Mr. Kupreskic, because you're telling us that, for instance, you were visited by two soldiers during the morning, rather early in the morning, two soldiers whose behaviour you said yesterday terrorised you. Although the location seemed very unsafe and very exposed, you still remained there, without moving, and without finding it necessary to go find your friends and your family in a place that was further removed. I don't understand why you remained at that location, all by yourself, and apparently in a position where you could be threatened by the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you see, of course I was afraid, because one of the soldiers took his gun off his shoulder and pointed it at me, asking me who I was. Of course I was afraid. But I brought some brandy for these people, they had a drink, and they went away again. So I stayed behind, and it's really hard to explain why, why I was there, except the reasons I have already given.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: As regards the two soldiers that you gave brandy to, did they tell you that they were members -- they told you they were members of the Jokers. Were you familiar with the Jokers? Did you know what that unit was?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I had heard that there was a unit called the Jokers, but I didn't know much more about them. I knew they were some kind of a special unit, and they told me that themselves that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Had you already gone past the Bungalow before the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I did go in that direction, beside the Bungalow, as well, and I saw that a unit was located there, of course, but I couldn't even now tell you which unit was there, but I did know that there was some sort of army in the Bungalow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke to us about Nikola Omazic. When you met him, how was Nikola Omazic dressed? Was he wearing a uniform or not? Was he carrying a weapon or not?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember what he was wearing. I think he did have a rifle. I think he had a rifle. He was a little tipsy and teetered around a bit, but I couldn't tell you how he was dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: From a document that was tendered in evidence during a previous hearing, P354, that Nikola Omazic, on that day, was in Ahmici. He was on duty with the HVO. What does this bring to your mind?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't think he was. I don't think he was on duty. I do know that I saw him for the first time at the entrance to the depression when I went to find people to help me take Mirjan Santic, who was already in my garage. When we brought him to the depression, Nikola, Zoran, Mirjan, and Dragan Vidovic took him off further. After that, I didn't see Nikola any more. Where he was, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, a witness who testified at this Tribunal under the pseudonym "H" stated that he saw on the 15th of April, 1993 -- that is, the day before the events that are of interest to us here -- that he saw HVO soldiers in front of your house, into which they were putting military-type equipment. What comment would you make about that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They could not have seen that at all because there was no military materiel in my house. Only trucks bringing goods came to my house which was to be sold, and to the warehouse, if Vlatko's premises and his warehouse at Veleprodaja was unable to take any more goods in. So all the goods that were superfluous, were surplus. They went to my premises, and no military materiel or weaponry was in my basement at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did your commercial activities ever have to do with military-type equipment? I'm not only speaking about weapons, weapons systems, but also other military equipment, such as uniforms, or all the objects that soldiers might need, soldiers who were on duty.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time, there was nothing interesting there. However, when the war ended, then some offers were coming in, and as there was a demand for military uniforms, my company too would offer military uniforms. But this was all in the course of 1994 and 1995 -- such as blankets and other coverings and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore, you never had any commercial activity in the -- that is, before April 1993 -- having to do with specifically military material and certainly not weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us that on several occasions during that day you saw Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. Do you remember how they were both dressed?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember. Mirjan had a civilian uniform, and Zoran had a camouflage shirt which was several sizes too large and could have fit me better than him. I think that he was wearing trousers as well -- jeans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In French, I heard "military uniform." Perhaps I'm wrong. Mirjan was wearing a military uniform; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I heard in French as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Whereas in the transcript it says "civilian uniform."

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let me ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, could you tell us again, as far as you remember, how Mirjan Kupreskic was dressed on that 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Civilian clothing, I said. But I used the term "civilian uniform." I used the term "uniform," but he was wearing civilian clothing, in fact. He had civilian clothing from head to foot. Zoran had a camouflage upper part, shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: This notion of a civilian uniform that you mentioned, was there such a thing?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it was -- what I had in mind was civilian clothing, in fact. I just used the wrong word and said "civilian uniform." I meant "civilian clothing."

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Were Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic armed on that 16th of April?
