utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Zoran had a hunting rifle, a carbine, and Mirjan had an M-48 rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Kupreskic, you were shown a document, a log, and you were asked to authenticate, if you could, the signature of Mirjan Kupreskic. On the document -- which is D352, unless I'm mistaken -- you asserted that this was not Mirjan Kupreskic's signature, and you told us that you were absolutely sure because as part of his professional activities in the Sutra company, Mirjan Kupreskic signed many documents. So here's my question: Did you bring to The Hague, or could you send to The Hague, perhaps through Mirjan Kupreskic's attorney, a specimen of Mirjan Kupreskic's handwriting?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have brought it with me, and you have it with the attorneys.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you know, are you in a position to identify the signature of Zoran Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I could not because I did not do anything specific, have any dealings with Zoran. But Mirjan would send papers to me every day with his signatures, and so I know his signature very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that you left Ahmici and that now you lived in Vitez, and that if you moved, it was largely connected to these events that we're speaking about, that's the events of 1993. You said that in the same way, the families of Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic lived in Vitez, and for the same reasons, apparently. Is there a reason why Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic and his family remained living in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really couldn't say why Vlatko stayed down there. That's his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, linked to the meeting that you mentioned and which took place on the terrace of your house after the first conflict, that is to say, in October 1992, tell us, please, you also mentioned that you know something about a decision about the return of rifles. What decision was that? What rifles, how many rifles? What decision?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that I have already said that. It was just mentioned, brought up at the meeting, the return of those rifles, and the decision was made at a previous meeting of some kind, and I said that what was in question were four rifles and that a vehicle had been confiscated at the roadblock down there. I really can't tell you any more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: (No translation)

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's what I heard, at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At that meeting, was it also decided that guards would be set up at the entrance to the village?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and I have already stated that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you recall what direction the meeting took? That is to say, what decisions were made, and whether there was any mention of any official type of decision. What was the tone, general tone of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I was a little late to arrive at the meeting because I was in Vitez, as I said, and my aunt phoned me there, so I turned up late, and they had already discussed matters, so that I was included at a belated date. We had a bottle of drink, we drank a little, and I suggested that if necessary, I would take the first shift doing the guard duty, and there wasn't to have been any problems along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would you once again repeat who was present from the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From the Muslim side there was Mr. Kalco Sulejman, the representative of the municipality --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And who was Mr. Kalco Sulejman in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was in charge, as far as I know, of the Defence Department or Office, something along those lines, as far as I know, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Kalco Sulejman was there for the Muslims. Who else was there of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic Fuad was there, and his brother Junuz, and Ahmic Zikrija, Sakib's son, who was a military man.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know in what capacity he attended the meeting? Was he in uniform? Was he a representative of the army? Was he there in any other capacity?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was he wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How do you know he was a military man at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I know that he had gone to military school within the system of the JNA, and I think that that is why he represented the army. I am trying to remember. I do actually think that he might have been wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know what he did otherwise?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well, no. Tell us, Ahmici, which municipality do they belong to?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They belong to the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what function did Pero Skopljak have?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't remember what function. I know that he had performed several functions, and at one time he was the chief of police. He was president of the HDZ for a time, but at that particular moment, I really don't know what functions he performed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did he take part in the municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was this authority established for Vitez, the town of Vitez proper, or for the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: For the municipality of Vitez, which is quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would you please indicate on the map the area in which the houses belonging to Jozo Vrebac are located, as well as Niko Vidovic and Milutin Vidovic. What part is it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is Jozo Vrebac's house (indicating), and that was the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, could you stand aside so that we can all see the aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is Milutin Vidovic's house (indicating), and that is the shelter and Jozo Vrebac's house (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what name does that part of the village go by?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That part of the village is called Santici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, in that part, the houses there, how many Muslims were there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, there were Muslims in this part as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I'm asking about the area you pointed out.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean this area here?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were no Muslim houses here. Only across the creek were there some Muslim houses. I think this was a Muslim house as well (indicating), and up here, in this section (indicating), where Balici --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In that overall area, that is to say, above the road, how many houses are there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In this entire part, this part here (indicating), there might be five or six houses, not more.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And how about the Croatian houses? How many, approximately?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There are many more Croatian houses. I don't know the exact number, but I think that there must be at least 50 households.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. You may sit down again. I'm sorry, while you're still standing, can you point out another place, where you saw Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: What do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I have in mind the 16th, the morning of the 16th, when they were on their way to the shelter.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it was approximately at Pudzine Kuce, in this part here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And you also stated that the army that you saw at Sakic's house, that it could have got there using different routes. Which routes existed in that part?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the map, you can see there is a road this way (indicating). They could have taken that route. They could have taken the upper route. There's a path here (indicating). There's a footpath running along here, and another little road here. There's a route here, a path, that is. So they could have used any of those paths, and they could have even come from this direction here, from this side, and used this road. They're all small paths that could have been used.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. You saw the direction in which they were moving. Where did you, in fact, see them? Was the first place by Niko Sakic's house?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the first time I saw them was there (indicating), and they went in the direction of the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You don't know which direction they actually had come from?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And you can't tell us that, can you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down again. Tell us, please, were you a member of the HDZ at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Zoran and Mirjan were members of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, they were certainly not, especially Zoran. Zoran had a lot of pressure exerted on him to join the HDZ. Most of the pressure was exerted on him by Slavko Milicevic. I think he came to visit him at least ten times to try and convince him to join the HDZ, however, he didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How do you know that? How do you know that Slavko Milicevic asked Zoran to join the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I knew that because I was present on several occasions when he called him up, and he said that they needed a man like him because he was an intellectual, he had graduated from university, so on and so forth, but each time, he would decline and did not want to accept.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the fact that Mirjan Kupreskic, while he worked for you, that is to say, after the war, had some contacts with Mr. Emir Perenda whom you mentioned. I think you said that you had a very large business, conducted a large business transaction for the Islamic community in 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Mirjan worked with me all the time, and on many occasions, he took Emir from Vitez to Travnik to his house there because Emir did not have a car of his own. He was included all the time, non-stop, and he would give goods to the Muslims with deferred payment. Sometimes I knew about this; sometimes I did not. One case in point was the person Mustafa Dzidic, called Dzida, who danced in the folklore group with him. He cried and said that his family would not be able to survive, and he prevailed upon him for two days. He asked me, and then Mirjan said okay, and he has never paid me for the goods until this day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: With reference to Emir Perenda, do you know him well?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I can say I know him well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you have a discussion with Emir Perenda concerning Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did talk about Mirjan Kupreskic with Emir Perenda. Emir Perenda only got to know Mirjan Kupreskic after the war, and he liked him as a person.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the fact that, as soon as this indictment was issued, Emir Perenda and Mirjan Kupreskic had a meeting --

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, after the indictment in '95, after Mirjan Kupreskic found out.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they did, and Emir was very surprised to hear that Mirjan Kupreskic was indicted, since he knew him well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did Emir Perenda talk about Mirjan Kupreskic's reaction to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. He said that he was very hard hit by it, which is quite logical, because, in my opinion, Mirjan should not be accused of such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: With reference to these activities of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic after the war, you said that you knew that both of them had worked. Can you say that Zoran Kupreskic also went abroad with a folk dancing group?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, because the Vitez folk dancing group could not be imagined without Zoran and Mirjan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just one more question: In connection with the jeans you bought at the market in 1992 --

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: -- who did you buy them from? Did you buy these jeans in a shop or from a private individual with a stall?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From a private individual who had a stall at the market.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At that time, was it usual for persons holding stalls at the market to be paid by bank transfers, for example, especially persons who were from another country, another state?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. At the market stalls, everything was paid for in cash, as it is today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: With reference to the negotiations you had in Koteks, Split --

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: -- you said you had some kind of memo?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I have my diary, my appointment book, because I never threw away these diaries, so I should have a diary. So it's a kind of business appointment book where you make notes of your business meetings, your business negotiations, whether a deal is concluded and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you think you haven't thrown it away?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think I haven't. I think it should be somewhere, but I can't be absolutely sure that I'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac. Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have only a brief clarification connected to D27/3, and I would like to ask the usher to put D27/3 on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, while the evidence is on its way, it follows from today's cross-examination that it is still unclear what border crossings were used and what routes. Since you marked the route you used from Vitez to Split and the route you returned by yesterday, I would now like to ask you to draw an arrow showing the direction of movement, showing, in fact, what route you took to reach Split ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Can you please stop? Could you please stop? Could we get this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: May we continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, could you please draw now, because I see that you have drawn an arrow showing the direction in which you moved from Vitez to Split, and could you put a "1" next to it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I see that you have already drawn in an arrow for your return journey. Could you mark it "2"?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We have no questions, Mr. Kupreskic. Thank you for testifying in court. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May we now move on to our next witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Vidovic. Could you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my colleague, Mr. Par, would like to join the examination-in-chief of this witness, my colleagues, Mr. Krajina and Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mrs. Vidovic. First of all, would you please introduce yourself to the Court? State your name, surname, your family's name, your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Ljuba Vidovic. I was born in 1944, on the 20th of May, in Busovaca, and I married in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you give us your present address?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I live in Santici, number 73, in my own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please say, in 1993, when the war broke out, were you married then or were you a widow?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was a widow at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many children you had?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Four children. I had a son and three daughters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: At the time the war broke out, who did you live with?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was living alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, we heard that you had a numerous family. Were there any victims in your family that were either killed or injured?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, my son-in-law was killed, then the sons of my other relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What about your granddaughter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: She lost her hand from a shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the centre of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did she stay alive?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. She's in Denmark now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Is she on her own or with her family?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: With her family, her father, her mother, and three sisters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Have you visited her?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I visited her in 1995. When she was asked what she wanted for Christmas, she said she wanted her grandmother. She kept asking for her grandmother, and then her father sent me money, he sent me 500 marks, so that I could come and visit my granddaughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: In Denmark, they are trying to rehabilitate her arm?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. She has an artificial hand, and they are treating her there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So she has obtained Danish citizenship?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and she is permanently resident there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: At the time just before the war, were you employed or were you a housewife?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was a housewife.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your education is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Primary school, five grades of primary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Were you interested in the political events?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was never interested in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the first conflict between the Muslims and the Croats in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that the Muslims set up roadblocks and that there was a little trouble, but it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything from your own observation about the first conflict?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I know my next door neighbour Reuf came to my house with his wife and children because he was afraid, so he spent the night at my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: That was during the first conflict?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the events between the first clash and the beginning of the war on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, village guards were established for security and because of the warplanes and the Serbian aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know any details?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was never interested in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what you were doing on the 15th of April, 1993, a day before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, who would remember? A housewife is a housewife. She thinks about what she's going to cook for her children.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, before the war broke out, was that day different in any way from all the other days preceding that day? Could you speak a little more slowly? Could there be a short break when I end my question for the interpreters? The question was: Was the day before the conflict broke out, as far as you were concerned, different in any way from all the other days?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was just an ordinary day, like every other day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did any of the neighbours warn you that dangerous days were coming?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us what happened on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But before we discuss that day, could you be so kind as to show us the location of your house on the map? You have an aerial photograph of Ahmici. Could you take the pointer and show it to us? Could you move a little and stand sideways so that the Judges can see?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is where Ante Vidovic's house is. This is Ivo Vidovic's house. This is Miso Lumic's house. This is Ramiz Ramic's house. This is my daughter's house. This is Reuf Podojak's, and this is my house. This is my brother-in-law's son's house and my other relative's house, and this is the house of my other relative (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Of all the houses you mentioned, could you repeat the names and indicate the houses of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the house of Ramo Ramic. This is Reuf Podojak's house (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: These are your only Muslim neighbours?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The house you pointed out as your house, was there only one house on that plot of land or were there two?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: One house. Where was your daughter's house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Across the road, above Ramo Ramic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Of my daughter? Lidija Sola.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Your house, your old house, to call it that, what quality was it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was an old house. It didn't have a concrete base. It was unsafe, so I moved into my daughter's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So there were wooden beams?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And your daughter's house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was a three-story house, and it had reinforced concrete parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did it have a basement?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When did you move into your daughter's house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When I returned from the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So until the beginning of the war, you lived in your own house, and when you came back from the shelter, for safety, you moved into your daughter's house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Where was your daughter at that time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Zenica. In Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did your daughter ever come from Zenica or did she spend the whole war in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: She spent the entire war in Zenica until there was a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us now what happened on the first day of the war at your place.

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the morning, at about 4.00 a.m., a soldier came and woke me up. I happened to look at my watch and saw that it was 4.00, and I was terrified. I said, "Why are you calling me? Who is it?" He said, "It's not important who it is. Go to a shelter. If you have livestock to tend to, do so, and then go to the shelter." When I had seen to my livestock and did everything that was necessary, there was no shooting yet, I went to the shelter --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Just slowly, please. The soldier who woke you up, what was that like? He knocked. Did he knock at the door, at the window?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He knocked at the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to understand, you opened the door?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What did you see outside the door? Did you switch the light on?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. He told me not to switch the light on but to open the door and not to be afraid and to get up. I went out. I didn't know the man. He was wearing a camouflage uniform. He had paint on his face. I didn't recognise him. He just said, "Tend to your livestock and go to the shelter."

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What did he look like, this soldier?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was covered over in paint and a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What was his face like?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was painted black.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the colour on his face?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember the colour on his face, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice whether the soldier was armed or not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if the truth be told, he did have a weapon of some kind, but I'm not very well up on weapons myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Was he alone or was there any other soldier with him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Was the soldier a local or was he totally unknown to you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was unknown. I had never seen him, nor did I know him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn who he was later on?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So that means that that soldier is still unknown to you; you never came to know who the soldier was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we now come to more concrete matters, and this will be a short witness. I think that we should continue after the break. We will get through this witness during the course of the day. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vidovic, we may continue. I think we left off talking about the first day of the war, the 16th of April, 1993, when you were woken up by an unknown soldier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: After he woke you up, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I went to the shed to tend to my livestock. When I had done everything necessary, I went to the shelter about 5.30, 6.00, and I saw a lot of people coming to the shelter there, women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What shelter was that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was at Jozo Vrebac's, that is to say, his daughter Jelena's place. That was the only large shelter and secure shelter in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you personally go to that special shelter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Because it was the safest one. It was dug into the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody direct you towards that shelter or did you conclude yourself that it was safest there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we went to that shelter when the air force was flying.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Which air force?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Communist Yugo Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what time did you arrive in the shelter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: 5.30, 6.00 a.m. I'm not quite sure. I didn't look at my watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find any people you knew in the shelter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I knew everybody because they were all local villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I am interested in knowing about Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. Did you see them anywhere?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When they came, that is to say, Mirjan with his wife Ljuba, and their two children came, and Zoran left Milutin, his wife, and children at Milutin Vidovic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that Zoran left his wife and children in Milutin's house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was on the pavement in front of the shelter when they came, and the house is near Milutin Vidovic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Then you saw that Zoran and his family had gone to Milutin Vidovic's house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What time was that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was about 6.00, a little before 6.00. I don't remember the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe how Mirjan was dressed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mirjan was dressed in civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What does that mean for you, "civilian"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it meant he wasn't -- not like a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And how was Zoran dressed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Zoran -- I saw Zoran when he came to visit his wife and children, and I saw that he had a camouflage jacket and had jeans, and a multi-coloured jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "multi-coloured jacket," is that part of a military uniform or is it a civilian jacket?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a multi-coloured -- I think camouflage, the type of camouflage jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You mean a part of a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall how many times on that particular day you saw Zoran Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Zoran and Mirjan came to see their wives and children about three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you say three times, you're talking about the first day of the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the first day of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the approximate time that you saw them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw them at about ten, one -- maybe half past three, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you have a watch, and were you able to tell us on the basis of the watch or just approximately?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the shelter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed in the shelter until 7 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I then went to my daughter's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in the shelter, did you hear any shooting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to determine the direction the shooting was coming from?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, who knows? When you're in a shelter, you have no idea what direction the shooting is coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can you determine when the shooting started, approximately?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At about 5.30, maybe, thereabouts. But I ran to the shelter between the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So as soon as you got to the shelter, the shooting started?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any flames, reflection of any fire which would lead you to conclude that houses were burning?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, you couldn't see whether houses were burning or not because we were on the other side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So you went home, and you went to your daughter's house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So that was also on the first day of the war, was it not? How come you dared, on the first day of the war, to go home at all?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm alone. I have small children, and there were a lot of people there, women and children, and so it was very noisy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: In the shelter, you mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So I went to my daughter's house because it was safe there. Then I went home, attended to the livestock, and saw Ramo Ramic standing at the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Who is Ramo Ramic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ramo Ramic is my next-door neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I asked him to come into my daughter's house, him and his wife. His child was in Zenica. He said, "I have six other wives and children," and that they could all come in, and they all did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (No translation)

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So all of them went to your house, did they? Is Ramo Ramic a Croat, or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What about the five or six people that came together with him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They're all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: They're all Muslims, you say. Thank you. During the time that these Muslims spent in your house, did anybody trouble them in any way?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Were you afraid because these people were in your house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I -- nobody troubled them. Of course, I -- and all our neighbours knew that the Muslims were in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And nobody made any trouble for you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody made any trouble for me, but I was not easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So this happened on the evening of the 16th or the 17th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, this was on the 17th. They came on the evening of the 16th, but this was on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What happened with the six Muslims who were in Ramo Ramic's house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As someone escorted them from this collection centre for Zenica, and the two of them stayed at my place, Ramo and his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So some of the people went to this collection centre. How many?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Six women and a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Are they all alive today?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Why did they leave your house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have enough space. It was a newly built house but was not completed yet and equipped.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You left Ramo Ramic and his wife, Mejra, nicknamed Dervisa. Did anybody come to your house on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The grandmother, Mejra Rasidovic. I know that we used to refer to her as Rasidoca.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And whose grandmother was she?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: She was Mejra's grandmother.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: She was whose mother?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: She was Mejra's mother's mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And what is Sakib Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sakib Ahmic is the son of this Rasidoca person.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So if I have understood correctly -- and please correct me if I'm wrong -- Sakib Ahmic's mother came to your place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, at that particular moment, your granddaughter was where?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At my daughter's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Together with her mother, you mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Together with her mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me now what Sakib Ahmic's mother looked like when she came?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: She was an old woman, dressed in the traditional Muslim woman's wear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of traditional Muslim wear was this?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, she had a scarf around her head, and she had the pantaloons that Muslim women wear, called dimija, the salvare type of pantaloon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What are they? They're a type of trousers, are they not, pantaloons, so you can describe them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they're broad pantaloons, the salvare type.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Sakib Ahmic from earlier on?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What did you know about him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I knew him as Sakib Ahmic. He was always there, his brothers were there, they were near us, and his sister's daughter, Mejra, was there, so I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But you weren't in any particularly friendly relations with him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we weren't friends and we weren't enemies. We just sort of -- you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What happened next, when Sakib Ahmic's mother came to your house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: She came in front of Mejra and Ramo's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Would you speak a little more slowly because this is an important part, and we would like it to be recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When the old woman came in front of Ramo Ramic's house, I happened to see her through the window, by chance, and I ran up to her. There was shooting, so I had to go around about and reach her that way. I told her, "Rasidoca," and she said "Ha," and said "Where is Ramo and Mejra?" I said, "They're at my place." So she kissed me, and I took her under her arm and led her to the house. She had something to drink, we made her a cup of coffee, let her rest up a little bit, and we bathed her lips. She was slightly wounded. She had been wounded by a bullet slightly, and I asked her whether she wanted a doctor. She said, "Don't bother calling a doctor. Just put something on it, on the wound." We bound it up, and she didn't want to see a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How long was the Rasidovic woman at your place?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: She stayed eight days, and on the ninth day she left.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: She went with who?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: With Mejra and Ramo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Where did they go to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They went to Zenica, to Perin Han.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I should just like to ask the witness about the people who took them to Zenica. So could we have a private session, that is to say, without sound, while I mention those particular names?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What is the name of the father of Mirko Sakic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: His name is Niko Sakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did you discuss -- what did you talk about with the mother of Sakib Ahmic? Did you discuss what was going on?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: On the first day of the war, and the time before she came to your place?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, when she had rested, we talked about how Sakib had come, and that when he was at the door she opened the door and said, "Is that you, my son?"

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Would you speak slowly, please, so that we can follow you. Would you tell us again?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When he came to his mother's house, he knocked on her door, and he said, "Open up, Mother." When she opened the door, she couldn't recognise him because he was burnt, charred a little bit. She said, "How come you're charred?" He said, "Well, I was under a haystack. Some of the soldiers had set light to the haystack, and I happened to be there." He took some socks -- she give him some socks and a pack of cigarettes, and then he left and went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did she tell you about what her son had told her about the fate of the individuals who were in his house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He said that he knew nothing, that he had escaped while the haystack was on fire, and that he went in the direction of the smoke so that he could not be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But did he not say what had happened to his son and daughter-in-law?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He said that his son had been killed somewhere on the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You don't recall the details?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. He said that his grandson and his son had been killed, but I don't remember him saying where.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What about his daughter-in-law?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell his mother who had done those things?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: His mother asked him who had done this, and he said, "Well, I can't say. I don't know."

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, did you ask her who did these acts or did she say it herself?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: She told us herself. Nobody asked her anything. She just talked about it herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, how did they learn about this discussion between you and Sakib Ahmic's mother?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was watching television, Bosnia-Herzegovina television, and the Tribunal and the trial, and Sakib Ahmic was a witness. When he said that Mirjan had given the petrol to Zoran and that they had set fire and that he was behind the couch, I went and told his mother this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What did you tell his mother?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that he was -- how his mother had said that he was by the haystack and not in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The television programme broadcast by Bosnia-Herzegovina, was it a programme called "The Hard Days," or "The Hague Hours," "The Hague Days," or something like that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, the story about Sakib Ahmic's mother is not quite clear to me in all its details. Could you tell us whether he had seen anything that had happened in his own house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He saw that his house was on fire and that his grandson and son had been killed. That's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But did he say where he was when his son and grandson had been killed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was under the haystack.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But how could he see what was happening in the house if he was under the haystack?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. That's what he told his mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Where was this haystack?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was by his house, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All right. What is important, in my opinion, is that she told Sakib's story and said that he did not know who had done this?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say whether Sakib Ahmic mentioned you in his testimony?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the newspaper, in Novi List of Rijeka, he mentioned me and my son, and said he had been saved by a Croatian woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the newspaper article referred to. It's from Novi List, which is published in Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D14/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Would you have a look at this article and say whether this is the article you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic, sorry to interrupt you. Could you please give us the date when this article was published?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The witness has only a cutting from the paper which we can show the Court, but this does not include a date. This was sent to me by my sister from Rijeka. It's just a clipping which arrived from Rijeka because the paper, Novi List, is not sold in the Vitez area. This was probably when Sakib Ahmic testified in the Blaskic case because that is when Bosnian Television broadcast his testimony, and in his testimony, he mentioned this lady as the woman who had saved his mother and some other Muslims. If you remember, when Sakib Ahmic testified before this Trial Chamber, he mentioned that his mother had stayed with this lady, so that now we have a witness here mentioned by Sakib Ahmic in his testimony, where he mentioned her as someone who had saved his mother and taken her in. I would like to conclude my questioning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Radovic. Counsel Par or Counsel Krajina? Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mrs. Vidovic, my name is Borislav Krajina, I'm a lawyer, defence counsel for the accused Vlatko Kupreskic. I will put a few questions to you in connection with the accused Vlatko Kupreskic. Would you please tell us, to begin with, whether you know Vlatko Kupreskic and --

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: -- would you wait until I finish, please? Do you know the members of his family and who do you know?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I know Vlatko, his wife, his children, his mother, and his father. I know them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Since when have you known them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ever since I married.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: When was that? How much time has passed since then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've known them since 1962 when I arrived in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Since 1962. Very well. You said that, in Jozo Vrebac's house or his daughter's house, you stayed in the shelter the whole day on the 16th of April, 1993, from about 6.00 a.m. until about 7.00 p.m.; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether you know or could you say before that whether you had been in the shelter throughout this time or whether you left the shelter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I ran to my shed to tend to my livestock twice, and each time, I was away for about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Very well. May we conclude then that you were in the shelter without interruption from 6.00 a.m. to 7.00 p.m. on the 16th of April, with two brief interruptions of about ten minutes each?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Very well. Would you now please tell us whether you saw any members of Vlatko Kupreskic's family in the shelter, and did you see Vlatko?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Who did you see?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I saw Vlatko, his wife, his children, and his mother, but his father stayed in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: When did you see them for the first time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the morning, they all came to the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: What time was it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, about half past five or six in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell us, if you remember, how Vlatko was dressed? Was he wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Was he armed perhaps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: No. Very well. Do you know how long Vlatko Kupreskic stayed in Jozo Vrebac's shelter that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He stayed -- since his late uncle Anto kept worrying about his brother, at about half past ten, eleven, he said, "I must go and see whether my father is still alive."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: So he left at about half past ten on that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Did you see him in the shelter again on that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, since I was there with them all. We were all in the shelter together. He came back and he said very happily, "My father is alive."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: When was that approximately?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon, about half past three or four. I don't remember exactly because I didn't look at my watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: So it was about half past three or four in the afternoon, and he said that about his father?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you found it strange? Because this was a shelter mainly for elderly people, women, children, people unfit to serve in the army, were you surprised to see Vlatko there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't surprised because Vlatko had a heart condition, and he was not fit for military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: So he wasn't fit for military service?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: I would like to ask you two or three further questions. Did you see Vlatko earlier before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Did you ever see him in a uniform or with weapons?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was engaged in trade and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Did you see him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would go to his shop to buy things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Very well. Can you say decidedly whether you ever saw him in a uniform or armed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Very well. Did you ever hear it rumoured in the village or do you know whether Vlatko was actively engaged in politics, whether he attended any political rallies, whether he belonged to any military units, and so on?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. He was interested only in his shop and his business. He wasn't interested in politics or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Can you say, as far as you know, if you do, what Vlatko's attitude was towards the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very good. They still come to his shop to buy things. When there was a cease-fire, they came to his shop to buy things, and I saw them there when I went there myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: I will be very brief, Mr. President, because a lot of questions have already been asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mrs. Vidovic, I will put just one more question to you connected with another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to go into closed session just during the answer to this question because we will mention a person who is a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Vidovic. My name is Franck Terrier. I'm one of the attorneys from the Office of the Prosecution. I'm going to ask you a few questions, and I don't think that it's going to take very long. First of all, I would like you to explain a point to me. We received, in respect of your testimony, two summaries, and the summaries differ a little, one from the other, on a point which, for me, is important, that is, the time that you were awoken on the 16th of April, 1993 and the time that you went to the shelter. In one of the summaries, it is stated that you were awoken at 4.00 in the morning on the 16th of April, which you confirmed a little while ago. The other summary states that, at 5.30, when the shooting began on Ahmici, you went to the Jozo Vrebac shelter. Could you solve this contradiction for us and tell us, very specifically or as specifically as your memory permits, what time you were awoken, alerted, on the 16th of April in the morning?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was awoken at 4.00, but by the time I had tended to the cattle in the shed, I didn't go to the shelter immediately, because when something happens, you know, you get lost. When I arrived exactly, it might have been half past five or six, because I had a calf, a cow, and some pigs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understand that it's difficult for you to give an exact time. Were you wearing a watch?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, but there was a clock in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could be more assertive in respect of the following point: You said, and I'm asking you to confirm this, you said that when you arrived in the shelter of Jozo Vrebac, the shooting had not yet begun. There was still silence over Santici, Ahmici, and Zume; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I said that I ran to the shelter when the shooting started. I was in the shed when the shooting started, and I ran between the houses, since it wasn't far to the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would like to insist upon this fact: Are you absolutely sure of your memories? Because in the two summaries that were given to us and which have to do with your testimony, it says that when you arrived -- well, you arrived at the Jozo Vrebac shelter before the shooting began?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I said that I was at home in the cowshed when the shooting started, and then I ran between the houses to the shelter as soon as the gunfire began.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: That means that there was a mistake in the summaries that were given to us. Likewise, in one of the summaries, you mentioned the way that you were awoken at 4.00 in the morning, and you speak about soldiers whose faces were covered about paint. You spoke about several soldiers, and a little while ago, you only spoke about a single soldier.

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was only one soldier. He woke me up, he was all painted, and I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But at that point, you only saw one soldier; you didn't see several soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Later on, during that day of 16 April, at any point during that day, did you see other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, because I was in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I would like the witness to be given Defence Exhibit D13/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vidovic, the house which is in this photograph and which you can see clearly in photograph 1, that is the house where you found shelter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Using these photographs to help yourself, could you tell us where you went in the house when you arrived on the 16th of April in the morning?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Down in the basement where these three doors are, down there. There are three doors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember what room you went into?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was a large room with women and children, and the adults were here in this anteroom, in the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You yourself, what room did you go into?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I personally, with my neighbours, was in the hallway, in this part here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The part that we can see in which photograph?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In front of that door, there was a hallway there as you go down the stairs. We didn't want to disturb the children who were lying down in the other room.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can we say that it's the part of the basement which we can see beyond the door which can be seen on photograph number 3?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You go down the steps, the stairs, and then it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And that's where you were?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Was there electric light there when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was electricity, but when the electricity was cut, then there wasn't any light anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Where you were, was there good light? Once the electric light went out, was there still good light?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you couldn't see much. We had to light candles. There were some tiny windows which gave us a bit of air at the top there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember when Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic and his family arrived? Specifically, his wife and children, when did they come?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They came straight after me, after me, to the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When you saw them coming, where were you? Were you in the location that you indicated a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was in front of the house number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in front of house number 1?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I stayed there an hour because there was shooting down over there, and Jozo's house was down there, so you couldn't go that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we've understood one another correctly. You told me that when you arrived, you went down into the basement and that there was light and then there wasn't any. Then you lit candles. Now you've just said that you stayed outside for an hour. I don't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That happened afterwards. When the light went out, we went down, and when we wanted to light up, we would go in front of the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But is your memory very clear, very precise? Since you were not yourself wearing a watch, are you exactly sure what time it was when you went back upstairs and how much time you spent down there? Do you have a very clear memory of all of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, who would remember everything that took place seven years ago, all the details and everything?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No. No, I understand, Mrs. Vidovic. That's why I'm asking you the question. I don't want you to say things or to have you say things that you can't say because it's very understandable, it's natural for you to have forgotten certain things. But I'm also asking that you not make specific assertions that do not correspond to your true memories. Therefore, is it true to say that you found shelter in that house and that you spent some time in the basement, you spent some time outside in front of the house, but you're no longer really in a position to say today what time you went down into the basement and what time you came back up or how long you spent in the basement and how much time you spent outside? All of that today is a little bit difficult to state, given the fact that, at that time, you didn't have a watch and given the amount of time that has elapsed since then. Is what I'm saying correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When I came to the shelter, the Kupreskic family arrived, and we all went through the same door. It was about six, half past five, six. I can't tell you the exact time. We then all went down to the shelter. When we wanted to light a cigarette, we would go out to smoke it, so that we were all there together, in contact together. We would see each other when we were going in and going out and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You're telling us now, Mrs. Vidovic, that you went down into the basement almost at the same time as Vlatko Kupreskic and his family and that Vlatko Kupreskic and his family stayed in the basement the way you did?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can I call your attention to the fact, Mrs. Vidovic, that we have a witness who was in that same house and that you probably noticed in the shelter, Mrs. Ankica Kupreskic, who noted the arrival of Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic and his family, but who told us that Vlatko Kupreskic had gone back upstairs and that he had not remained in the basement, that only his wife and children had remained. Does this match your memory of that same event?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He stayed in front of the door, and we went down to the shelter. He was there all the time until his uncle Ante began crying and asking what had happened to his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vidovic, it's very difficult to be specific, given the amount of time that has elapsed and also given the circumstances that you experienced, which must have been very, very difficult, but you have just said that Vlatko Kupreskic, if I've understood what you said, remained outside the house in front of the door of the house while you were going down into the shelter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. He would go down and go up. We were not all in the same place. You couldn't sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore, Vlatko Kupreskic, according to what you just said now, did not remain in the basement of the house until the time that you indicated a little while ago, until 10.00, that he didn't remain until 10.00?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you yourself remain in the basement of the house that whole time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Fifteen minutes, ten minutes, five minutes, it was that far from my house to there to tend to the cattle, but when I came, I saw him, and it was before 11.00. It was about 10.00 when his uncle told him to go and see what was happening to his father, and we just happened to glance at a watch -- a clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You said that you didn't have a watch.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's either a watch or a clock in the shelter. Interpreter's note: "Sat," "watch" or "clock."

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would like you to speak about your neighbour, Ramo Ramic, who greeted you at your house on the evening of the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us a little while ago that Mr. Ramo Ramic's house and his family's house was destroyed the next day on the 17th of April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In your opinion, why was the house destroyed on that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't know. Unfortunately, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: On the 16th or 17th of April, did you see your other Muslim neighbour, Reuf Podojak, and his family?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the same day, they went towards Poculica, on the 16th at about 9.00 or 10.00. I don't exactly. I don't know exactly, but they left, and they are all alive and well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did they leave voluntarily or were they forced to leave?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When you met and then received at your house Sakib Ahmic's mother, what mental state was she in?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: She was in a terrible state. She's an old woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How old was she in 1993?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, she was over 70 at the time. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore, in respect of what Sakib Ahmic allegedly said to his mother, you remember what his mother said, who was about 70 years old and who was in a very difficult mental state, one can understand that, and you are telling us what you remember today about what that woman said.

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When she had washed up a bit and had something to eat, then she told us herself. We didn't ask her how Sakib had come to her place and what he had experienced, what I said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But did her account seem very exact to you, extremely clear? Did she seem to you to have a very clear idea about what had happened? Was she really affirmative in her statements?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as we didn't ask her and she said what she said herself, when I saw it on television afterwards, it sort of got me, and I told their mother, Luca Kupreskic, whom I had known for many years. I was upset that these innocent kids were locked up (in jail).

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you still live in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Santici, number 73.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you still live in the same place that you lived at that time, in the same house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, I was at my daughter's house. As a shell fell in front of my own house, the glass was shattered. Now the house has been rebuilt, and I'm in my own house now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you very much, Mrs. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I will put just a few questions to you to try to clarify some points. Can you tell us what Mejra was to Sakib, what relation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mejra's mother and Sakib were brother and sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So Mejra, what is she to Sakib?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: She is his cousin, his sister's daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So he is her uncle?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you were talking to Sakib Ahmic's mother, did you start the conversation about Sakib or did she initiate the conversation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: She told us of her own accord. When she had had a good rest, then she started talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When she began her story, did she tell the whole story or did you interrupt her with questions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. She just talked of her own accord.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did she perhaps explain to you when her son Sakib visited her -- where exactly is her house; do you know?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Her house is in Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Her house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How far is it, as the crow flies, from your house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, some 500 metres perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: It's a bit longer if you take the path?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But it's downhill, as far as I could gather?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I live there, and so I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether she explained why her son Sakib came to her house, to his old mother living on her own, and why he left his elderly mother alone in the house and didn't take her with him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what she was wondering. He only asked for some socks and some cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did she tell you that, while Sakib was finishing his visit with her, shooting had already started in the direction of her house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, she didn't tell us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But she herself could not explain why her son was fleeing and leaving her behind?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, she couldn't explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: As regards the Prosecutor's questions, can you tell us what your relations were with your Muslim neighbours?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Your Croat neighbours, as far as you know, what relations did they have with their Muslim neighbours?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We would all invite each other over. We would ask them over for Christmas, and they would ask us over for Bajram.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you or any of your Croat neighbours do anything to drive away your Muslim neighbours?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: God forbid, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Was it your will and the will of your Croatian neighbours to make the Muslims go away?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I'm concerned, and I can speak about my neighbours, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: I have only two short questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mrs. Vidovic, please, at the time from about half past five to six in the morning until half past ten, while you were in the shelter or in front of the shelter where the adults, as you say, would go in and out to smoke a cigarette, were you there all the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said, I left for a brief period because it's some five, ten minutes away to my stable, and I ran to tend to my livestock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: When was it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't keep looking at the clock, or watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Could you tell us, on the basis of your testimony, could you confirm with certainty that Vlatko Kupreskic was with his family in that shelter on the 16th of April, without interruption, from about 6.00 a.m. to about half past 10.00?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: And that he didn't leave the place in front of the shelter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Only when he went to see whether his father was alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: That was about half past 11.00. What about until then? Was he there all the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBA VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We have no questions. Mrs. Vidovic, thank you so much for coming to The Hague to give evidence in court. You may now be released. We are adjourned now until tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 1.30 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of March, 1999, at 9.00 a.m.
